new_statements.quote: In Arrernte, stress is assigned within a word to the first nucleus that is preceded by a consonant. Thus, if the word begins in a consonant, stress falls on the first vowel; if the word begins in a vowel, stress falls on the second nucleus (vowel) in that word. (2) a. ikwén't' 'policeman' b. atwérem 'is fighting' c. Nén.irem 'are standing' d. mpwár.em 'is making/doing' If consonant-initial words, such as those in (2c–d), are indeed underlyingly /e/-initial, then stress in Arrernte falls on the second syllable and is computed at some level where the initial /e/ is present.
new_statements.citation: Breen, Gavan & Rob Pensalfini. 1999. Arrernte: a language with no syllable onsets. Linguistic Inquiry 30(1): 1-25.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Western Arrernte has an empty rule and there are no existing stress statements, so this supplies the placement: first vowel preceded by a consonant (= second underlying syllable). It agrees with Anderson 2000 (UCLA dissertation on Western Arrernte, downloaded in the 2026-09-16 pass, printed p. 41: 'Primary stress generally falls on the first syllable containing an onset'); Anderson adds alternating secondary stress and the /#aCe/ variation from Wilkins 1989, which Breen & Pensalfini do not mention. Note the article's data are from Eastern/Central Arrernte varieties (Henderson & Dobson 1994, Green 1994, Wilkins 1989); the authors state in fn. 5 that the analysis applie…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress goes to the first vowel that has a consonant before it: the first vowel of a word pronounced with an initial consonant, the second vowel of a word pronounced with an initial vowel. Under the authors' own analysis, in which every Arrernte word is underlyingly vowel-initial (initial /e/ deletes phrase-initially), this is simply stress on the second underlying syllable, computed before the initial /e/ is lost. The article treats this onset-sensitive surface pattern as an argument for underlying initial vowels rather than for onset-sensitive stress (Davis 1988, Goedemans 1996). Pages 8-9 describe the same pattern as an Arandic areal feature: 'stress (on polysyllables) on the second vowel or the first vowel following a consonant'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; the article mentions only 'a primary stressed vowel' (Appendix A, p. 22) and never states where secondary stress falls.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 2: the optional phrase-final vowel [U] 'may be stressed on occasion, as when it is the only vowel in the utterance (in this case it is normally somewhat lower, so that /mpe/ "come on" is pronounced [mbá])'. Footnote 5 (p. 4): 'Davis suggests this for a different dialect than the one our analysis is based on, but we believe our analysis applies to that dialect, Western Arrernte, too.' No other exceptions or lexical irregularities are given.
new_statements.identity_note: Breen & Pensalfini 1999 do not name their variety in the body; the data and references (Henderson & Dobson 1994 Eastern and Central Arrernte dictionary, Green 1994, Wilkins 1989 Mparntwe Arrernte, Breen 1990) point to Eastern/Central (Mparntwe) Arrernte, and footnote 21 (p. 21) defines 'variety' by the five areas of Henderson & Dobson 1994:9. Footnote 5 (p. 4) explicitly says the stress analysis is based on 'a different dialect' from Davis's (1988) Western Arrernte but that the authors believe it applies to Western Arrernte too. Appendix A (p. 22) mentions 'the neighboring dialects Western and Southern Arrernte'. So the statement is offered for Arrernte generally, Western Arrernte included, but the primary data are Eastern/Central Arrernte (Glottolog would put that under east2380/Eastern Arrernte rather than west2441).

The primary Western Aranda description (Strehlow 1942/1944, 224 pp, accentuation pp.46-50) is not yet obtained and not open; no instrumental study of WAr stress exists in Glottolog's list or the cached OpenAlex scan. sources.quote: "Primary stress generally falls on the first syllable containing an onset, with secondary stress being associated with every other following syllable, except the final syllable. Wilkins (1989) mentions one source of counter-examples of the shape /#aCe/ [a-C-schwa], in which stress may fall on either /e/, which has the onset, or the initial /a/. Thus, 'Arrernte' can be either [a'r...] or ['ar...]. Moreover, there is evidence that both /a/ and /i/ seem to attract stress even where they are not initial ... 'fingernail' can be produced as ['tapmaya] ... or [tap'maya] ... Breen accounts for default
